prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In spite of the large number of papers appeared in the past which are devoted to the lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods, basic aspects of the theory still remain unchallenged. An unsolved theoretical issue is related to the construction of a discrete kinetic theory which yields \textit{exactly} the fluid equations, i.e., is non-asymptotic (here denoted as \textit{LB inverse kinetic theory}). The purpose of this paper is theoretical and aims at developing an inverse kinetic approach of this type. In principle infinite solutions exist to this problem but the freedom can be exploited in order to meet important requirements. In particular, the discrete kinetic theory can be defined so that it yields exactly the fluid equation also for arbitrary non-equilibrium (but suitably smooth) kinetic distribution functions and arbitrarily close to the boundary of the fluid domain. Unlike previous entropic LB methods the theorem can be obtained without functional constraints on the class of the initial distribution functions. Possible realizations of the theory and asymptotic approximations are provided which permit to determine the fluid equations \textit{with prescribed accuracy.} As a result, asymptotic accuracy estimates of customary LB approaches and comparisons with the Chorin artificial compressibility method are discussed.

outputs.L1:
Despite the large number of papers published in recent years on lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods, fundamental aspects of the theory remain unresolved. One outstanding theoretical issue concerns the construction of a discrete kinetic theory that yields the fluid equations \textit{exactly}, i.e., in a non-asymptotic sense, here referred to as the \textit{LB inverse kinetic theory}. The purpose of this paper is theoretical: it aims to develop an inverse kinetic approach of this kind.

In principle, infinitely many solutions to this problem exist; however, this freedom can be exploited to satisfy important requirements. In particular, the discrete kinetic theory can be formulated so as to reproduce exactly the fluid equations also for arbitrary non-equilibrium, but suitably smooth, kinetic distribution functions and at points arbitrarily close to the boundary of the fluid domain. Unlike previous entropic LB methods, the theorem can be established without imposing functional constraints on the class of initial distribution functions.

Possible realizations of the theory and asymptotic approximations are presented, allowing the fluid equations to be determined \textit{with prescribed accuracy}. As a result, asymptotic accuracy estimates of customary LB approaches are discussed, together with comparisons to the Chorin artificial compressibility method.
outputs.L2:
Although many papers have been published over the years on lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods, several fundamental elements of the theory have not yet been fully addressed. One unresolved theoretical problem concerns how to formulate a discrete kinetic theory that reproduces the fluid equations exactly, rather than only in an asymptotic limit; this is referred to here as an LB inverse kinetic theory. The aim of the present work is theoretical: to develop such an inverse kinetic formulation.  

In principle, this problem admits infinitely many possible solutions, and this non-uniqueness can be used advantageously to satisfy significant conditions. Specifically, the discrete kinetic model may be constructed so that it recovers the fluid equations exactly even for arbitrary non-equilibrium kinetic distribution functions, provided they are sufficiently smooth, and even at locations arbitrarily near the boundary of the fluid domain. In contrast with earlier entropic LB approaches, the theorem can be established without imposing functional restrictions on the admissible initial distribution functions.  

The paper also presents possible implementations of the theory and asymptotic approximations that allow the fluid equations to be obtained with a prescribed level of accuracy. Consequently, it discusses asymptotic error estimates for standard LB methods and compares them with Chorin’s artificial compressibility method.
outputs.L3:
The paper addresses an unresolved theoretical issue in lattice Boltzmann methods: how to construct a discrete kinetic theory that reproduces the fluid equations exactly, rather than only in an asymptotic or approximate sense. Traditional lattice Boltzmann approaches typically recover macroscopic fluid equations through limiting procedures, such as low-Mach-number or Chapman–Enskog expansions. As a result, the correspondence between the discrete kinetic model and the target fluid equations is often approximate and may depend on assumptions about scale separation, smoothness, or proximity to equilibrium.

To overcome this limitation, the paper proposes a lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic theory. This framework is specifically designed so that the prescribed macroscopic fluid equations are recovered exactly and non-asymptotically from the kinetic description. In particular, the method is formulated to yield the exact fluid equations for arbitrary, suitably smooth non-equilibrium kinetic distribution functions. This means that the validity of the macroscopic equations does not depend on the distribution function being close to an equilibrium state, nor on the use of perturbative expansions.

A further important feature of the proposed theory is that it remains applicable arbitrarily close to the boundary of the fluid domain. Boundary regions are often a source of difficulty in lattice Boltzmann methods, since discrete velocity sets and boundary conditions can introduce errors or require special treatments. The ability of the inverse kinetic theory to operate near boundaries strengthens its relevance for realistic fluid-dynamical problems, where accurate boundary behavior is essential.

The approach also differs significantly from earlier entropic lattice Boltzmann methods. Entropic methods generally impose functional constraints on the initial kinetic distribution functions, often to ensure positivity, entropy consistency, or nonlinear stability. By contrast, the inverse kinetic theory presented in the paper does not require such constraints on the initial distributions. This gives the formulation greater flexibility and broadens the class of admissible kinetic states from which the exact fluid equations can be recovered.

Finally, the paper discusses possible realizations of the theory, along with asymptotic approximations that make the approach practically usable. These approximations allow the fluid equations to be determined with a prescribed level of accuracy, thereby connecting the exact theoretical framework with implementable numerical schemes. In this way, the work provides both a conceptual resolution to a fundamental problem in lattice Boltzmann theory and a pathway toward practical computational applications.

The paper addresses a still unresolved issue in lattice Boltzmann theory: how to construct a genuinely non-asymptotic inverse kinetic formulation based on a discrete velocity set that exactly reproduces the prescribed fluid equations. In standard lattice Boltzmann approaches, the recovery of the macroscopic equations is often obtained only in an asymptotic sense, for example through Chapman–Enskog expansions or small-Mach-number limits. By contrast, the objective of an inverse kinetic theory is to design a kinetic equation whose velocity moments reproduce the target fluid equations exactly, without relying on such limiting procedures.

A central observation of the paper is that there is not a unique discrete kinetic formulation capable of producing the same macroscopic dynamics. Rather, there exists an infinite family of possible lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic theories. This freedom can be exploited to impose additional requirements on the kinetic model. In particular, the formulation can be chosen so that it remains valid in the presence of boundaries, is compatible with smooth non-equilibrium distribution functions, and avoids restrictions that would otherwise limit its applicability. The paper therefore investigates how to select, among the many possible discrete kinetic descriptions, those that satisfy physically and mathematically desirable conditions.

The authors show that a non-asymptotic lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic theory can indeed be constructed. This theory exactly recovers the intended fluid equations at the level of the relevant kinetic moments. Importantly, the construction does not require the functional constraints that are typical of entropic lattice Boltzmann methods, where the distribution functions are often constrained by entropy principles or by special admissibility conditions. Instead, the proposed formulation uses the available freedom in the kinetic representation to obtain exact moment closure while preserving a broad class of admissible smooth distributions.

The paper also discusses explicit realizations of the theory. These realizations demonstrate how suitable discrete kinetic equations can be built in practice and how the corresponding moment equations reproduce the desired macroscopic fluid system. In addition to exact formulations, the authors consider asymptotic approximations of the non-asymptotic theory. These approximations can be constructed with prescribed accuracy, making it possible to control the error introduced by simplified lattice Boltzmann schemes. The analysis thereby clarifies how accuracy estimates should be understood in this framework and how they differ from the estimates usually associated with conventional asymptotic lattice Boltzmann methods.

Finally, the work establishes connections with Chorin’s artificial compressibility method. By comparing the inverse kinetic formulation with artificial compressibility ideas, the paper places the proposed lattice Boltzmann theory in a broader numerical and analytical context. It shows that certain approximate forms of the theory can be interpreted as kinetic counterparts of artificial compressibility schemes, while the full non-asymptotic formulation provides a more exact representation of the target fluid equations. Overall, the paper presents a framework for constructing lattice Boltzmann models that are exact at the macroscopic level, flexible at the kinetic level, and capable of systematic approximation with controlled accuracy.
outputs.L5:
**The Legacy of Boltzmann**

The physicist Ludwig Boltzmann changed the way scientists understand heat, energy, and matter. Unlike earlier theories that treated temperature as a simple property of objects, Boltzmann showed that it could be explained through the motion of countless tiny particles. His work helped build the foundation of statistical mechanics, a field that connects the behavior of atoms and molecules with the large-scale world we can observe.

The importance of Boltzmann’s ideas lies in their ability to explain order and disorder. He showed that natural processes tend to move toward states that are more probable, helping to clarify the meaning of entropy. Unlike simple mechanical descriptions, his theory embraced probability as a key part of physics.

Today, Boltzmann’s influence can be seen in physics, chemistry, information theory, and even modern computing. The concepts he developed continue to help scientists understand complex systems, from gases and liquids to stars and biological processes. His work remains a powerful reminder that the visible world is shaped by invisible motion.

The approach constructs a discrete kinetic model whose velocity moments are constrained to reproduce the target macroscopic balance laws identically at the level of the discrete evolution equation. By formulating the collision operator and equilibrium structure through moment-inversion conditions, the resulting lattice Boltzmann dynamics is shown to provide an exact kinetic representation of the governing fluid equations, rather than an approximation derived from Chapman–Enskog analysis. The theory clarifies the relationship between discrete velocity sets, moment closure, forcing terms, and macroscopic consistency, and establishes conditions under which incompressible and compressible fluid models can be embedded in a finite-dimensional kinetic system. Particular attention is given to the role of non-hydrodynamic moments and gauge freedoms in ensuring realizability, stability-compatible relaxation, and exact recovery of pressure and momentum dynamics. The framework offers a systematic route for deriving lattice Boltzmann schemes from prescribed continuum equations and provides a basis for analyzing their consistency independently of asymptotic scaling arguments. This inverse construction suggests new possibilities for exact fluid solvers based on discrete kinetic representations and contributes to the mathematical foundations of lattice Boltzmann methodology.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an abstract in the style of a mathematical physics journal article on unresolved theoretical issues in lattice Boltzmann methods, focusing on exact recovery of fluid equations and comparison with Chorin artificial compressibility.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**  
We examine unresolved theoretical questions concerning the status of lattice Boltzmann methods as discrete kinetic representations of incompressible fluid dynamics. Particular attention is given to the problem of *exact* recovery of the Navier–Stokes equations from finite-velocity, finite-lattice schemes, as distinct from their formal recovery through Chapman–Enskog or diffusive asymptotic expansions. While standard lattice Boltzmann models reproduce the incompressible equations to leading order in a low-Mach-number scaling, residual compressibility, finite-lattice anisotropy, non-Galilean invariant truncation errors, and boundary-induced defects indicate that the equivalence is generally asymptotic rather than exact. We discuss the role of moment closure, quadrature constraints, collision-operator structure, and relaxation spectra in determining whether a lattice kinetic scheme can be interpreted as an exact discretization of a target hydrodynamic system or only as a controlled approximation.

The analysis is contrasted with Chorin’s artificial compressibility formulation, which also replaces the incompressibility constraint by an evolution equation for pressure. In Chorin’s method, the artificial sound speed and pseudo-time relaxation are introduced explicitly as numerical devices whose incompressible limit is obtained by a singular perturbation. Lattice Boltzmann methods possess an analogous weakly compressible structure, but the artificial compressibility is embedded in the discrete kinetic equation through the equation of state, lattice sound speed, and equilibrium distribution. This comparison clarifies both the practical similarity and the theoretical distinction between the two approaches: Chorin’s scheme approximates the incompressible equations by augmenting them at the macroscopic level, whereas lattice Boltzmann methods seek to obtain them as emergent moment equations from a mesoscopic dynamics.

We identify several open issues: the existence of nontrivial finite lattice Boltzmann models yielding exact incompressible Navier–Stokes dynamics without asymptotic limiting procedures; the mathematical characterization of consistency beyond formal multiscale expansions; the influence of discrete velocity quadrature on nonlinear momentum transport; and the extent to which pressure projection, artificial compressibility, and kinetic relaxation represent equivalent mechanisms in the incompressible limit. These questions remain central to a rigorous foundation of lattice Boltzmann methodology and to the interpretation of its accuracy, stability, and physical fidelity in simulations of fluid flows.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract**—This paper establishes a non-uniqueness result for inverse kinetic lattice Boltzmann formulations of prescribed macroscopic evolution equations. We show that, for a given target continuum model and a fixed set of kinetic moments reproducing its macroscopic fields, there exist infinitely many discrete kinetic representations whose moment equations yield the same prescribed dynamics. The resulting freedom may be characterized through arbitrary higher-order moments, collision/source parametrizations, and equilibrium or non-equilibrium extensions that are invisible to the recovered macroscopic balance laws. Rather than constituting an ambiguity to be eliminated, this non-uniqueness provides a constructive design mechanism. In particular, we demonstrate that the free functional and algebraic degrees of freedom can be selected to enforce additional regularity of the kinetic populations, compatibility with boundary data, and prescribed accuracy requirements at the kinetic or macroscopic level. The analysis clarifies the distinction between macroscopic consistency and kinetic realization, showing that inverse lattice Boltzmann schemes form an infinite-dimensional admissible class constrained only by moment closure, solvability, and the chosen discrete velocity set. These results provide a systematic basis for designing tailored inverse kinetic lattice Boltzmann methods with improved smoothness, boundary behavior, and error-control properties while preserving the exact recovery of the target macroscopic equations.
